source.title: Not All Samples Should Be Utilized Equally: Towards Understanding and Improving Dataset Distillation
source.authors: Shao-Bo Wang; Yan-Tai Yang; Qi-Long Wang; Kaixin Li; Lin-Feng Zhang; Jun-Chi Yan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study adapts a data-pruning scaling theory to dataset distillation and reports its own theoretical and simulation findings, which qualify how scaling behavior carries over to that setting.
record.gate_note: Theoretical and simulation results on perceptron test error versus synthetic sample count bear on V5. The paper's gradient-norm observations and SDC accuracy gains across image datasets are not rows: they assess sample difficulty or the proposed method, not whether the scaling law holds. Scaling results cited from other work are also excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows Sorscher et al.'s perceptron data-pruning theory to explain dataset distillation and motivate its SDC regularizer. Its only power-law statement (ε ∝ αsyn^-1 at f = 1) is the textbook perceptron learning curve, which the paper reproduces as a reference rather than tests. Rows r2–r3 compare hard-sample versus no-distillation strategies; they say nothing about whether a power law holds. Nothing bears on loss scaling in parameters, tokens or compute, or on power-law form in image models. The image experiments report only SDC accuracy gains.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, but incomplete. The authors also report that GM-based methods raise gradient norms (harder samples) while TM-based methods lower them. They propose Sample Difficulty Correction (a gradient-norm regularizer) and report it improves accuracy across 7 distillation methods and 6 image datasets, especially at low IPC.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a statistical-mechanics expert-student perceptron analysis and numerical simulations of synthetic dataset distillation, rather than language-model pretraining loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior varies with synthetic sample ratio αsyn and sample difficulty (hard versus easy); the theory also considers probe angle γ.

fits_no_version.finding: In the perceptron theory, synthesizing from hard samples is worse than no distillation at small αsyn and substantially better at large αsyn. Easy samples are preferred in the small-data regime.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal sample-difficulty strategy for data pruning or distillation depends on the retained-data-to-parameter ratio (easy samples when data are scarce, hard samples when abundant).

record.problems: The scaling analysis is theoretical and simulation-based in a toy perceptron setting with Gaussian inputs; it does not establish scaling behavior for trained image models. The relevant curve results are primarily presented graphically, and the text gives no fitted power-law exponents for the distilled-data cases.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law results omitted. The paper's SDC and ASDC test-accuracy tables and figures are excluded because they evaluate the proposed regularizer, not scaling-law behavior.

untested.parts: All: language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
All: no power-law fit in image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. The toy perceptron curve is a reproduced textbook result.
All: fit dependence of exponents or allocation.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation. The study is a dataset-distillation method paper that uses scaling-law theory as an explanatory tool, so no verdicts are given. The reader's V5 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of architecture depth, width, or other details at fixed parameter count.
The study analyzes a toy perceptron dataset-distillation setting; it does not test image or video model scaling, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on parameter counting, schedules, data, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: expert-student perceptron
rows.stage_stated: Student trained on the synthetic dataset; f = 1 is no distillation.
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed test error as synthetic samples per parameter αsyn varies, in the no-distillation case.
rows.measure: Test error ε versus synthetic samples per parameter αsyn
rows.note: The text identifies this as the classical perceptron learning power-law scaling. The result is a no-distillation reference condition.
rows.check: This is the classical perceptron learning-curve result inherited from Sorscher et al. (cited theory), stated as a reference condition with no fitted exponent. It is a Gaussian-input toy perceptron, not a new modality or training regime of the kind V5 names, so it is not a test of V5.

rows.subject: expert-student perceptron
rows.stage_stated: Student trained on the synthetic dataset.
rows.operation_detail: Compared distillation from hard samples with the no-distillation reference as αsyn varies.
rows.value: Hard-sample learning gives poorer performance than no distillation.
rows.note: The text says small αsyn corresponds to small synthetic datasets, typical of low-IPC distillation.
rows.check: This compares a sample-selection strategy (hard samples) with no distillation at small αsyn. It does not measure whether a power law holds. It is a finding about distillation strategy, not scaling-law form.

rows.subject: expert-student perceptron
rows.stage_stated: Student trained on the synthetic dataset.
rows.operation_detail: Compared distillation from hard samples with the no-distillation reference as αsyn varies.
rows.value: Focusing on hard samples yields substantially better outcomes than no distillation.
rows.note: The reported change with αsyn means the preferred distillation strategy depends on synthetic dataset size; the text does not give numerical values for these comparisons.
rows.check: Same as r2, at large αsyn. It is a strategy comparison, not a measure of power-law scaling. The 'partial' state against V5 was unfounded.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: No-distillation reference in the toy perceptron setting
reader_labels.reason: The study reports the classical inverse power law for test error in this reference condition (r1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Toy perceptron dataset distillation, varying αsyn
reader_labels.reason: The reported hard-sample outcome changes with synthetic dataset size: it is worse than no distillation at small αsyn and substantially better at large αsyn (r2–r3), so the extension is not a single size-independent rule.
